e-12567.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $\mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+t^2\,\mathbf j+t^3\,\mathbf k$ at the point $P(1,1,1).$
e-12567.worked_solution:
The point $P(1,1,1)$ is at the tip of $\mathbf r(t)$ for some specific value $t_0$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point,  the vector $\mathbf r'(t_0)$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\,i+\,j+\,k \\ t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j+{t}^{3}\,k & =i+\,j+\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $\mathbf i, \mathbf j,$ and $\mathbf k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}t=1 \\ {t}^{2}=1 \\ {t}^{3}=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(1,1,1)$ is at the tip of the vector $\mathbf r(1).$  

Now, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,k \\  & =i+2t\,j+3{t}^{2}\,k \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =i+2(1)\,j+3(1)^{2}\,k \\  & =i+2\,j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at at the point $P(1,1,1)$ is $\,\mathbf i+2\,\mathbf j+3\,\mathbf k.$

e-12568.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve
e-12568.problem: Find a parametrization of the tangent line to the curve $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle \cos{t}, \: \sin{t},\: 4t^2\right\rangle$ at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$
e-12568.worked_solution:
Let  $P$ be the point at the tip of the vector $\mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right ).$  At this point,  the vector $\mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right )$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
\mathbf R(u)=\mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right )+u \, \mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right ), \qquad u \in (-\infty, \infty).
$$

 

First, we find $\mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,4{(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}⟩=⟨0,1,{\pi }^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now,  we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,8t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,8(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0,4\pi ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P$ where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(u)=⟨0,1,{\pi }^{2}⟩+u⟨-1,0,4\pi ⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14049728/assets/e24b811fb8d9e43bd0682e3686f8b2ef1198e36016978ca305a7df4dffe21889.png)

e-12580.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to Another Vector
e-12580.problem: Given the curve $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle t^2+1\,,\, 6t+3\right\rangle,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $\left\langle 3\,,\, 1\right\rangle.$
e-12580.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t+3)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\,,\,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $\left\langle 3\,,\, 1 \right\rangle$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $\left\langle 3\,,\, 1 \right\rangle \cdot \mathbf r'(t) = 0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨3\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨3\,,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨2t\,,\,6⟩ & =0 \\ 3\cdot 2t+1\cdot 6 & =0 \\ 6t+6 & =0 \\ t & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨(-1)^{2}+1\,,\,6(-1)+3⟩=⟨2\,,\,-3⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $\left\langle 3\,,\, 1\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(2,-3).$

e-12569.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Parallel to Another Vector
e-12569.problem: Given the curve $\mathbf r(t)=(t^2+t)\,\mathbf i+(t^2-t)\,\mathbf j,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $3\, \mathbf i+\,\mathbf j.$
e-12569.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,j \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(2t-1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $3\, \mathbf i+\,\mathbf j$ are parallel for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $\mathbf r'(t)=c(3\, \mathbf i+\,\mathbf j).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(2t+1)\,i+(2t-1)\,j=c(3\,i+\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf j$ gives the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2t+1=3c \\ 2t-1=c\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $c=2t-1.$ Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2t+1 & =3c \\ 2t+1 & =3(2t-1) \\ 2t+1 & =6t-3 \\ 6t-2t & =1+3 \\ 4t & =4 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\mathbf r'$ and $3\, \mathbf i+\,\mathbf j$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =({1}^{2}+1)\,i+({1}^{2}-1)\,j=2\,i,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $3\, \mathbf i+\,\mathbf j$ are parallel at the point $(2,0).$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=(1-t)\,i-{t}^{2}\,j+(2t+1)\,k$ at the point $P(2,-1,-1).$
after.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,-1,-1)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point, the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i-j-k \\ (1-t)\,i-{t}^{2}\,j+(2t+1)\,k & =2\,i-j-k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}1-t=2 \\ -{t}^{2}=-1 \\ 2t+1=-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=-1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,-1,-1)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(-1).$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+1)\,k \\  & =-i-2t\,j+2\,k \\ {r}^{′}(-1) & =-i-2(-1)\,j+2\,k \\  & =-i+2\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point $P(2,-1,-1)$ is $-i+2\,j+2\,k.$

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Vector
content.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=(1-t)\,i-{t}^{2}\,j+(2t+1)\,k$ at the point $P(2,-1,-1).$
content.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,-1,-1)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point, the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i-j-k \\ (1-t)\,i-{t}^{2}\,j+(2t+1)\,k & =2\,i-j-k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}1-t=2 \\ -{t}^{2}=-1 \\ 2t+1=-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=-1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,-1,-1)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(-1).$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+1)\,k \\  & =-i-2t\,j+2\,k \\ {r}^{′}(-1) & =-i-2(-1)\,j+2\,k \\  & =-i+2\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point $P(2,-1,-1)$ is $-i+2\,j+2\,k.$

decision.explanation: Differentiating gives r'(t)=sec(t)tan(t)i+sec²(t)j+k. At t=π/4, sec(t)=√2 and tan(t)=1, so a tangent vector is √2 i+2j+k, option d.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,j+t\,k$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
after.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sec}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{tan}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,i+{sec}^{2}⁡t\,j+\,k \\ {r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}\,i+{sec}^{2}⁡\frac{\pi }{4}\,j+\,k \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,i+2\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$  is  $\sqrt{2}\,i+2\,j+\,k.$

a
2i+2j+k

2i+j+k
c
2i−2j+k
d
2i+2j+k
e
2i+2j+k

Correct
EXPLANATION

At the point where t=π4, the vector r′(π4) is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate r′(t) and evaluate it at t=π4: r′(t)=ddt(sec⁡t)i+ddt(tan⁡t)j+ddt(t)k=sec⁡ttan⁡ti+sec2⁡tj+kr′(π4)=sec⁡π4tan⁡π4i+sec2⁡π4j+k=2i+2j+k

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where t=π4 is 2i+2j+k.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Find a vector that's tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨t+\frac{1}{t},\,t-\frac{1}{t}⟩$ at the point where $t=1.$
after.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=1$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(1)$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+\frac{1}{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\frac{1}{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨1-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨1-\frac{1}{{1}^{2}},\,1+\frac{1}{{1}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨1-1,\,1+1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=1$  is  $⟨0,\,2⟩.$

At the point where t=π, the vector r′(π) is tangent to the curve.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=(3t+2)\,i+(6t+1)\,j+(1-4{t}^{2})\,k$ at the point $P(2,1,1).$
after.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,1,1)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point, the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i+j+k \\ (3t+2)\,i+(6t+1)\,j+(1-4{t}^{2})\,k & =2\,i+j+k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}3t+2=2 \\ 6t+1=1 \\ 1-4{t}^{2}=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,1,1)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(0).$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t+1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-4{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =3\,i+6\,j-8t\,k \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =3\,i+6\,j-8(0)\,k \\  & =3\,i+6\,j\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Vector
content.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=(3t+2)\,i+(6t+1)\,j+(1-4{t}^{2})\,k$ at the point $P(2,1,1).$
content.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,1,1)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point, the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i+j+k \\ (3t+2)\,i+(6t+1)\,j+(1-4{t}^{2})\,k & =2\,i+j+k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}3t+2=2 \\ 6t+1=1 \\ 1-4{t}^{2}=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,1,1)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(0).$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t+1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-4{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =3\,i+6\,j-8t\,k \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =3\,i+6\,j-8(0)\,k \\  & =3\,i+6\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point $P(2,1,1)$ is $3\,i+6\,j.$

before.html:
Question 6
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=(t2−1)i+1+t2j+(t−1)k at the point corresponding to t=2, valid for all real values of u?

a
3i+5j+k+u(5i+15j+k)
b
3i+5j+k+u(4i+45j+k)
c
3i+5j+k+u(5i+25j+2k)
d
3i+5j+k+u(4i+25j+2k)
e
3i+5j+k+u(4i+25j+k)
Submit

decision.explanation: The tangent line is R(u)=r(2)+u r'(2). Here r(2)=3i+√5 j+k and r'(t)=2t i+(t/√(1+t²))j+k, so r'(2)=4i+(2/√5)j+k. Thus option e gives the tangent line for every real u.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=({t}^{2}-1)\,i+\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,j+(t-1)\,k$ at the point corresponding to $t=2,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
after.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=2$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(2)$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r(2)+u{r}^{′}(2),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

First, we find $r(2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =({2}^{2}-1)\,i+\sqrt{1+{2}^{2}}\,j+(2-1)\,k \\  & =3\,i+\sqrt{5}\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)\,k \\  & =2t\,i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(2) & =2(2)\,i+\frac{(2)}{\sqrt{1+(2)^{2}}}\,j+\,k \\  & =4\,i+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point 
 where $t=2$ is 

$$
R(u)=3i+\sqrt{5}\,j+\,k+u(4\,i+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\,j+\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Question 6
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=(t2−1)i+1+t2j+(t−1)k at the point corresponding to t=2, valid for all real values of u?

a
3i+5j+k+u(5i+15j+k)
b
3i+5j+k+u(4i+45j+k)
c
3i+5j+k+u(5i+25j+2k)
d
3i+5j+k+u(4i+25j+2k)
e
3i+5j+k+u(4i+25j+k)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

At the point where t=2, the vector r′(2) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as

R(u)=r(2)+ur′(2),u∈(−∞,∞).

First, we find r(2): r(2)=(22−1)i+1+22j+(2−1)k=3i+5j+k

Now, we calculate r′(t):

r′(t)=ddt(t2−1)i+ddt(1+t2)j+ddt(t−1)k=2ti+t1+t2j+k

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=2:

r′(2)=2(2)i+(2)1+(2)2j+k=4i+25j+k Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where t=2 is R(u)=3i+5j+k+u(4i+25j+k),u∈(−∞,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve
content.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=({t}^{2}-1)\,i+\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,j+(t-1)\,k$ at the point corresponding to $t=2,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
content.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=2$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(2)$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r(2)+u{r}^{′}(2),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

First, we find $r(2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =({2}^{2}-1)\,i+\sqrt{1+{2}^{2}}\,j+(2-1)\,k \\  & =3\,i+\sqrt{5}\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)\,k \\  & =2t\,i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(2) & =2(2)\,i+\frac{(2)}{\sqrt{1+(2)^{2}}}\,j+\,k \\  & =4\,i+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point 
 where $t=2$ is 

$$
R(u)=3i+\sqrt{5}\,j+\,k+u(4\,i+\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\,j+\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

before.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=⟨cos⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩ at the point where t=π, valid for all real values of u?

a
⟨1,1⟩+u⟨−1,0⟩
b
⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩
c
⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨−1,0⟩
d
⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨−1,1⟩
e
⟨1,1⟩+u⟨0,1⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: At t=π, r(π)=⟨−1,0⟩. Differentiating gives r'(t)=⟨−sin(t),−cos(t)⟩, so r'(π)=⟨0,1⟩. The tangent line is therefore ⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩ for all real u, matching option b.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ at the point where $t=\pi ,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
after.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\pi ,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(\pi )+u{r}^{′}(\pi ),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\pi ) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=\pi $ is

$$
R(u)=⟨-1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).

Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=⟨cos⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩ at the point where t=π, valid for all real values of u?

a
⟨1,1⟩+u⟨−1,0⟩
b
⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩
c
⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨−1,0⟩
d
⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨−1,1⟩
e
⟨1,1⟩+u⟨0,1⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

At the point where t=π, the vector r′(π) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as R(u)=r(π)+ur′(π),u∈(−∞,∞)

First, we find r(π): r(π)=⟨cos⁡π,−sin⁡π⟩=⟨−1,0⟩

Now, we calculate r′(t): r′(t)=⟨ddt(cos⁡t),ddt(−sin⁡t)⟩=⟨−sin⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=π: r′(π)=⟨−sin⁡π,−cos⁡π⟩=⟨0,1⟩

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where t=π is
R(u)=⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩,u∈(−∞,∞).

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms r(π)=⟨−1,0⟩ and r'(π)=⟨0,1⟩. Therefore the tangent line is ⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩ for all real u, option b. The deliberately submitted option e has the wrong base point.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve
content.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ at the point where $t=\pi ,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
content.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\pi ,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(\pi )+u{r}^{′}(\pi ),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\pi ) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=\pi $ is

$$
R(u)=⟨-1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Question 8
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=1+ti+(t2−5)j+(3t−1)k at the point P(2,4,8), valid for all real values of u?

a
2i+4j+8k+u(i+6j+6k)
b
2i+4j+8k+u(14i+6j+3k)
c
2i+4j+8k+u(14i+3j−3k)
d
2i+4j+8k+u(i+6j+3k)
e
2i+4j+8k+u(14i−6j−3k)
Submit

decision.explanation: The point P corresponds to t=3, since r(3)=(2,4,8). Differentiating gives r'(t)=(1/(2√(1+t)))i+2t j+3k, hence r'(3)=(1/4)i+6j+3k. The tangent line is P+u r'(3) for all real u, matching option b.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve  $r(t)=\sqrt{1+t}\,i+({t}^{2}-5)\,j+(3t-1)\,k$ at the point $P(2,4,8),$  valid for all real values of $u?$
after.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,4,8)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

where ${t}_{0}$ corresponds to the value of $t$ at the point $P.$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i+4\,j+8\,k \\ \sqrt{1+t}\,i+({t}^{2}-5)\,j+(3t-1)\,k & =2\,i+4\,j+8\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+t}=2 \\ {t}^{2}-5=4 \\ 3t-1=8\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the third equation, we get $t=3.$ This value also satifies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,4,8)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(3).$  

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{1+t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-5)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-1)\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+t}}\,i+2t\,j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(3) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+(3)}}\,i+2(3)\,j+3\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}\,i+2\cdot 3\,j+3\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,i+6\,j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P(2,4,8)$ is

$$
R(u)=2i+4\,j+8\,k+u(\frac{1}{4}\,i+6\,j+3\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Question 8
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=1+ti+(t2−5)j+(3t−1)k at the point P(2,4,8), valid for all real values of u?

a
2i+4j+8k+u(i+6j+6k)
b
2i+4j+8k+u(14i+6j+3k)
c
2i+4j+8k+u(14i+3j−3k)
d
2i+4j+8k+u(i+6j+3k)
e
2i+4j+8k+u(14i−6j−3k)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The point P(2,4,8) is at the tip of r(t) for some specific value t0 of the parameter t. At this point the vector r′(t0) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as

R(u)=r(t0)+ur′(t0),u∈(−∞,∞),

where t0 corresponds to the value of t at the point P.

First, we find the value of t that corresponds to P. We know that:

r(t)=2i+4j+8k1+ti+(t2−5)j+(3t−1)k=2i+4j+8k,

and equating the coefficients of i,j, and k yields the following system:

{1+t=2t2−5=43t−1=8

From the third equation, we get t=3. This value also satifies the other two equations. Therefore, P(2,4,8) is at the tip of the vector r(3).

We calculate r′(t):
r′(t)=ddt(1+t)i+ddt(t2−5)j+ddt(3t−1)k=121+ti+2tj+3k

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=3:

r′(3)=121+(3)i+2(3)j+3k=124i+2⋅3j+3k=14i+6j+3k

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point P(2,4,8) is
R(u)=2i+4j+8k+u(14i+6j+3k),u∈(−∞,∞).

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

where ${t}_{0}$ corresponds to the value of $t$ at the point $P.$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i+4\,j+8\,k \\ \sqrt{1+t}\,i+({t}^{2}-5)\,j+(3t-1)\,k & =2\,i+4\,j+8\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+t}=2 \\ {t}^{2}-5=4 \\ 3t-1=8\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the third equation, we get $t=3.$ This value also satifies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,4,8)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(3).$  

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{1+t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-5)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-1)\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+t}}\,i+2t\,j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(3) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+(3)}}\,i+2(3)\,j+3\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}\,i+2\cdot 3\,j+3\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,i+6\,j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P(2,4,8)$ is

$$
R(u)=2i+4\,j+8\,k+u(\frac{1}{4}\,i+6\,j+3\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

before.html:
Question 9
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=2sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj+sin2tk at the point corresponding to t=π4, valid for all real values of u?

a
i+j+12k+u(i−j+12k)
b
i+j+12k+u(2i−j+k)
c
i+j+12k+u(−i+2j+k)
d
i+j+12k+u(i+2j+12k)
e
i+j+12k+u(i−j+k)
Submit

decision.explanation: At t=π/4, r(t)=i+j+(1/2)k. Differentiating gives r'(t)=√2 cos(t)i−√2 sin(t)j+2sin(t)cos(t)k, so r'(π/4)=i−j+k. Thus r(π/4)+u r'(π/4) matches option e for all real u.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+{sin}^{2}t\,k$ at the point corresponding to $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
after.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

 

$$
R(u)=r(\frac{\pi }{4})+u{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j+{sin}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})\,k \\  & =\,i+\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{2}t)\,k \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j-\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})k \\  & =\,i-\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point 
 where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
R(u)=\,i+\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k+u(\,i-\,j+\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Question 9
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=2sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj+sin2tk at the point corresponding to t=π4, valid for all real values of u?

a
i+j+12k+u(i−j+12k)
b
i+j+12k+u(2i−j+k)
c
i+j+12k+u(−i+2j+k)
d
i+j+12k+u(i+2j+12k)
e
i+j+12k+u(i−j+k)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

At the point where t=π4, the vector r′(π4) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as

R(u)=r(π4)+ur′(π4),u∈(−∞,∞)

First, we find r(π4):

r(π4)=2sin⁡(π4)i+2cos⁡(π4)j+sin2(π4)k=i+j+12k

Now, we calculate r′(t):

r′(t)=ddt(2sin⁡t)i+ddt(2cos⁡t)j+ddt(sin2t)k=2cos⁡ti−2sin⁡tj+2sin⁡tcos⁡tk

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=π4:

r′(π4)=2cos⁡(π4)i+2sin⁡(π4)j−2sin⁡(π4)cos⁡(π4)k=i−j+k

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where t=π4 is
R(u)=i+j+12k+u(i−j+k),u∈(−∞,∞).

verification.explanation: Direct differentiation gives r'(π/4)=i−j+k, and r(π/4)=i+j+(1/2)k. Thus option e is correct and matches the worked solution's conclusion. Its intermediate substitution contains sign typos; the derivative formula and final result are correct.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve
content.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+{sin}^{2}t\,k$ at the point corresponding to $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
content.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

 

$$
R(u)=r(\frac{\pi }{4})+u{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j+{sin}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})\,k \\  & =\,i+\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{2}t)\,k \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j-\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})k \\  & =\,i-\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point 
 where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
R(u)=\,i+\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k+u(\,i-\,j+\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

before.html:
Question 10
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=eti+3tj+cos⁡2tk at the point corresponding to t=π, valid for all real values of u?

a
eπi+3πj+k+u(eπi+j)
b
eπi+3πj+k+u(eπi+3j)
c
eπi+3πj+k+u(eπi+j+2k)
d
eπi+3πj+k+u(eπi+3j+2k)
e
eπi+3πj+k+u(eπi+3j+k)
Submit

decision.explanation: At t=π, r(π)=e^π i+3π j+k. Differentiating gives r'(t)=e^t i+3j−2sin(2t)k, so r'(π)=e^π i+3j. The tangent line r(π)+u r'(π), for all real u, is option b.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)={e}^{t}\,i+3t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,k$ at the point corresponding to $t=\pi ,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
after.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\pi $,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r(\pi )+u{r}^{′}(\pi ),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\pi ) & ={e}^{\pi }\,i+3(\pi )\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡2(\pi )\,k \\  & ={e}^{\pi }\,i+3\pi \,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,k \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i+3\,j-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi ) & ={e}^{(\pi )}\,i+3\,j+\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡2(\pi )k \\  & ={e}^{\pi }\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point 
 where $t=\pi $ is 

$$
R(u)={e}^{\pi }\,i+3\pi \,j+\,k+u({e}^{\pi }\,i+3\,j),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Question 10
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=eti+3tj+cos⁡2tk at the point corresponding to t=π, valid for all real values of u?

a
eπi+3πj+k+u(eπi+j)
b
eπi+3πj+k+u(eπi+3j)

At the point where t=π, the vector r′(π) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as R(u)=r(π)+ur′(π),u∈(−∞,∞)

First, we find r(π): r(π)=eπi+3(π)j+cos⁡2(π)k=eπi+3πj+k

Now, we calculate r′(t):

r′(t)=ddt(et)i+ddt(3t)j+ddt(cos⁡2t)k=eti+3j−2sin⁡2tk

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=π:

r′(π)=e(π)i+3j+2sin⁡2(π)k=eπi+3j

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where t=π is R(u)=eπi+3πj+k+u(eπi+3j),u∈(−∞,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve
content.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)={e}^{t}\,i+3t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,k$ at the point corresponding to $t=\pi ,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
content.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\pi $,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r(\pi )+u{r}^{′}(\pi ),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\pi ) & ={e}^{\pi }\,i+3(\pi )\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡2(\pi )\,k \\  & ={e}^{\pi }\,i+3\pi \,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,k \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i+3\,j-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi ) & ={e}^{(\pi )}\,i+3\,j+\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡2(\pi )k \\  & ={e}^{\pi }\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point 
 where $t=\pi $ is 

$$
R(u)={e}^{\pi }\,i+3\pi \,j+\,k+u({e}^{\pi }\,i+3\,j),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=t\,i+\frac{1}{t}\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,j \\  & =i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [t\,i+\frac{1}{t}\,j]\cdot (i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j) & =0 \\ t\cdot 1-\frac{1}{t}\cdot \frac{1}{{t}^{2}} & =0 \\ t-\frac{1}{{t}^{3}} & =0 \\ {t}^{4} & =1 \\ t & =\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $t=\pm 1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1)=1\,i+\frac{1}{1}\,j=\,i+j, \\ r(-1)=(-1)\,i+\frac{1}{(-1)}\,j=-\,i-j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the points $(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1).$

\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,j \\  & =i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [t\,i+\frac{1}{t}\,j]\cdot (i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j) & =0 \\ t\cdot 1-\frac{1}{t}\cdot \frac{1}{{t}^{2}} & =0 \\ t-\frac{1}{{t}^{3}} & =0 \\ {t}^{4} & =1 \\ t & =\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $t=\pm 1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1)=1\,i+\frac{1}{1}\,j=\,i+j, \\ r(-1)=(-1)\,i+\frac{1}{(-1)}\,j=-\,i-j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the points $(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1).$

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨1-{t}^{2},3t+4⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨1,1⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2t,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $⟨1,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨1,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨1,1⟩\cdot ⟨-2t,3⟩ & =0 \\ 1(-2t)+1(3) & =0 \\ -2t+3 & =0 \\ t & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=\frac{3}{2}.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{3}{2}) & =⟨1-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2},3(\frac{3}{2})+4⟩ \\  & =⟨1-\frac{9}{4},\frac{9}{2}+4⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{5}{4},\frac{17}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(-\frac{5}{4},\frac{17}{2}).$

Given the curve r(t)=⟨1−t2,3t+4⟩, find the point at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector ⟨1,1⟩.

a
(34,112)
b
(112,58)
c
(32,114)
d
(−54,172)
e
(112,54)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t): r′(t)=⟨ddt(1−t2),ddt(3t+4)⟩=⟨−2t,3⟩

The vectors ⟨1,1⟩ and r′(t) are perpendicular for some value of the parameter t if and only if ⟨1,1⟩⋅r′(t)=0. So, we have ⟨1,1⟩⋅r′(t)=0⟨1,1⟩⋅⟨−2t,3⟩=01(−2t)+1(3)=0−2t+3=0t=32.

Therefore, the only solution is t=32.

Finally, since r(32)=⟨1−(32)2,3(32)+4⟩=⟨1−94,92+4⟩=⟨−54,172⟩, we conclude that ⟨1,1⟩ and r′(t) are perpendicular at the point (−54,172).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to Another Vector
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨1-{t}^{2},3t+4⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨1,1⟩.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2t,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $⟨1,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨1,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨1,1⟩\cdot ⟨-2t,3⟩ & =0 \\ 1(-2t)+1(3) & =0 \\ -2t+3 & =0 \\ t & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=\frac{3}{2}.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{3}{2}) & =⟨1-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2},3(\frac{3}{2})+4⟩ \\  & =⟨1-\frac{9}{4},\frac{9}{2}+4⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{5}{4},\frac{17}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(-\frac{5}{4},\frac{17}{2}).$

Question 13
?

Given the curve r(t)=⟨2t5,t2−2⟩, t∈(0,∞), find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector ⟨1,−5⟩.

a
 (64,2)
b
 (64,2) and (116,−74)
c
 (2,−1)
d
 (2,−1) and (116,−74)
e
(116,−74)
Submit

decision.explanation: The tangent vector is r'(t)=⟨10t⁴,2t⟩. Its dot product with ⟨1,−5⟩ is 10t⁴−10t=10t(t³−1). Since t>0, this vanishes only at t=1. Therefore the only point is r(1)=(2,−1), option c.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨2{t}^{5}\,,\,{t}^{2}-2⟩,$ $t\in (0,\infty ),$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨1\,,\,-5⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{5})\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2)⟩ \\  & =⟨10{t}^{4}\,,\,2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨1\,,\,-5⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨1\,,\,-5⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1\,,\,-5⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨1\,,\,-5⟩\cdot ⟨10{t}^{4}\,,\,2t⟩ & =0 \\ 1\cdot 10{t}^{4}+(-5)\cdot 2t & =0 \\ 10{t}^{4}-10t & =0 \\ 10t({t}^{3}-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (0,\infty )$, the only solution is $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨2(1)^{5}\,,\,(1)^{2}-2⟩=⟨2\,,\,-1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $⟨1\,,\,-5⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(2\,,\,-1).$

Question 13
?

Given the curve r(t)=⟨2t5,t2−2⟩, t∈(0,∞), find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector ⟨1,−5⟩.

a
 (64,2)
b
 (64,2) and (116,−74)
c
 (2,−1)
d
 (2,−1) and (116,−74)
e
(116,−74)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t): r′(t)=⟨ddt(2t5),ddt(t2−2)⟩=⟨10t4,2t⟩

The vectors ⟨1,−5⟩ and r′(t) are perpendicular for some value of the parameter t if and only if ⟨1,−5⟩⋅r′(t)=0. So, we have

⟨1,−5⟩⋅r′(t)=0⟨1,−5⟩⋅⟨10t4,2t⟩=01⋅10t4+(−5)⋅2t=010t4−10t=010t(t3−1)=0.

Since t∈(0,∞), the only solution is t=1.

Finally, since

r(1)=⟨2(1)5,(1)2−2⟩=⟨2,−1⟩,

we conclude that ⟨1,−5⟩ and r′(t) are perpendicular at the point (2,−1).

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms r'(t)=⟨10t⁴,2t⟩. Perpendicularity requires 10t⁴−10t=10t(t³−1)=0. On t>0, only t=1 qualifies, giving r(1)=(2,−1). Thus option c contains all qualifying points.

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to Another Vector
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨2{t}^{5}\,,\,{t}^{2}-2⟩,$ $t\in (0,\infty ),$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨1\,,\,-5⟩.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{5})\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2)⟩ \\  & =⟨10{t}^{4}\,,\,2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨1\,,\,-5⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨1\,,\,-5⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1\,,\,-5⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨1\,,\,-5⟩\cdot ⟨10{t}^{4}\,,\,2t⟩ & =0 \\ 1\cdot 10{t}^{4}+(-5)\cdot 2t & =0 \\ 10{t}^{4}-10t & =0 \\ 10t({t}^{3}-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (0,\infty )$, the only solution is $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨2(1)^{5}\,,\,(1)^{2}-2⟩=⟨2\,,\,-1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $⟨1\,,\,-5⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(2\,,\,-1).$

Question 14
?

Given the curve r(t)=ti+(1+12t2)j, find all of the points at which r′(t) and r(t) are perpendicular.

a
(0,1)
b
(2,3)
c
(2,3) and (−2,3)
d
(0,1), (2,2), and (−2,2)
e
(0,1) and (2,3)
Submit

decision.explanation: Differentiating gives r'(t)=⟨1,t⟩. The dot product r(t)·r'(t)=t+t(1+t²/2)=t(2+t²/2) vanishes only at t=0 for real t. Thus the only point is r(0)=(0,1), option a.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=t\,i+(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [t\,i+(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\,j]\cdot (i+t\,j) & =0 \\ t\cdot 1+(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\cdot t & =0 \\ 2t+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{3} & =0 \\ t(4+{t}^{2}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=0$ since $4+{t}^{2}>0$ for any $t.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)=0\,i+(1+\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})\,j=j,\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

Given the curve r(t)=ti+(1+12t2)j, find all of the points at which r′(t) and r(t) are perpendicular.

a
(0,1)
b
(2,3)
c
(2,3) and (−2,3)
d
(0,1), (2,2), and (−2,2)
e
(0,1) and (2,3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t): r′(t)=ddt(t)i+ddt(1+12t2)j=i+tj

The vectors r(t) and r′(t) are perpendicular for some value of the parameter t if and only if r(t)⋅r′(t)=0. So, we have

r(t)⋅r′(t)=0[ti+(1+12t2)j]⋅(i+tj)=0t⋅1+(1+12t2)⋅t=02t+12t3=0t(4+t2)=0.

Therefore, the only solution is t=0 since 4+t2>0 for any t.

Finally, since

r(0)=0i+(1+12(0)2)j=j,

we conclude that r(t) and r′(t) are perpendicular at the point (0,1).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to Another Vector
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=t\,i+(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [t\,i+(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\,j]\cdot (i+t\,j) & =0 \\ t\cdot 1+(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\cdot t & =0 \\ 2t+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{3} & =0 \\ t(4+{t}^{2}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=0$ since $4+{t}^{2}>0$ for any $t.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)=0\,i+(1+\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})\,j=j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(0,1).$

Given the curve r(t)=(t2−8)i−4tj, find all of the points at which r′(t) and r(t) are perpendicular.

a
 (−8,0) and (−7,−4)
b
 (9,12)
c
 (−4,8) and (9,12)
d
 (−7,−4) and (−4,−8)
e
(−8,0)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t): r′(t)=ddt(t2−8)i+ddt(−4t)j=2ti−4j

The vectors r(t) and r′(t) are perpendicular for some value of the parameter t if and only if r(t)⋅r′(t)=0. So, we have

r(t)⋅r′(t)=0[(t2−8)i−4tj]⋅(2ti−4j)=0(t2−8)⋅2t+(−4t)⋅(−4)=02t3−16t+16t=02t3=0.

Therefore, the only solution is t=0.

Finally, since

r(0)=(02−8)i−4(0)j=−8i,

we conclude that r(t) and r′(t) are perpendicular at the point (−8,0).

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨1,3t²,2t⟩. If r(t)=c r'(t), the first component gives c=t. The other components require 2+t³=3t³ and 1+t²=2t², so t³=1 and t²=1. Their only common real solution is t=1, giving r(1)=(1,3,2), option a.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=t\,i+(2+{t}^{3})\,j+(1+{t}^{2})\,k$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$   

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+{t}^{3})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =i+\,3{t}^{2}\,j+\,2t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ t\,i+(2+{t}^{3})\,j+(1+{t}^{2})\,k & =c(i+\,3{t}^{2}\,j+\,2t\,k).\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}t=c \\ 2+{t}^{3}=c(3{t}^{2}) \\ 1+{t}^{2}=c(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation we obtain $t=c.$ Substituting $c=t$ into the second equality gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}2+{t}^{3} & =3{t}^{3} \\ 2 & =2{t}^{3} \\ {t}^{3} & =1 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This satisfies also the equation $1+{t}^{2}=c(2t).$
Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =i+(2+{1}^{3})\,j+(1+{1}^{2})\,k \\  & =i+3\,j+2\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $P(1,3,2).$

Question 16

Given the curve r(t)=ti+(2+t3)j+(1+t2)k, find all points at which r′(t) and r(t) are parallel.

a
(1,3,2)
b
(0,2,1)
c
(1,3,2) and (−1,3,2)
d
(2,10,5)
e
(0,2,1) and (−1,1,2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t):

r′(t)=ddt(t)i+ddt(2+t3)j+ddt(1+t2)k=i+3t2j+2tk

The vectors r′(t) and r(t) are parallel for some specific value t0 of the parameter t if and only if there exists a constant c such that r(t0)=cr′(t0). So, we have

r(t)=cr′(t)ti+(2+t3)j+(1+t2)k=c(i+3t2j+2tk).

Equating the coefficients of i,j, and k gives:

{t=c2+t3=c(3t2)1+t2=c(2t)

From the first equation we obtain t=c. Substituting c=t into the second equality gives

2+t3=3t32=2t3t3=1t=1

This satisfies also the equation 1+t2=c(2t). Therefore, r and r′ are parallel only at the point corresponding to t=1.

Finally, since r(1)=i+(2+13)j+(1+12)k=i+3j+2k, we conclude that r(t) and r′(t) are parallel at the point P(1,3,2).

Question 17
?

Given the curve r(t)=e2ti+(t2+t+12)j, find all points at which r′(t) and r(t) are parallel.

a
(1,12) and (e2,52)
b
(e,54) and (e−2,12)
c
(1,12)
d
(e2,52)
e
(e,54)
Submit

decision.explanation: Differentiating gives r'(t)=⟨2e^(2t),2t+1⟩. Since e^(2t)>0, parallelism requires r'(t)=2r(t). Thus 2t+1=2(t²+t+1/2), which reduces to 2t²=0. Only t=0 qualifies, giving r(0)=(1,1/2), option c.

after.name: Question 17
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)={e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =c(2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =2c{e}^{2t}\,i+c(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j$ gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}=2c{e}^{2t} \\ {t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2}=c(2t+1)\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain $c=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting $c=\frac{1}{2}$ into the second equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(2t+1) \\ {t}^{2} & =0 \\ t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel at the point corresponding to $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & ={e}^{0}\,i+({0}^{2}+0+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =i+\frac{1}{2}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,\frac{1}{2}).$

Given the curve r(t)=e2ti+(t2+t+12)j, find all points at which r′(t) and r(t) are parallel.

a
(1,12) and (e2,52)
b
(e,54) and (e−2,12)
c
(1,12)
d
(e2,52)
e
(e,54)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t):

r′(t)=ddt(e2t)i+ddt(t2+t+12)j=2e2ti+(2t+1)j.

The vectors r′(t) and r(t) are parallel for some specific value t0 of the parameter t if and only if there exists a constant c such that r(t0)=cr′(t0). So, we have

r(t)=cr′(t)e2ti+(t2+t+12)j=c(2e2ti+(2t+1)j)e2ti+(t2+t+12)j=2ce2ti+c(2t+1)j.

Equating the coefficients of i and j gives:

{e2t=2ce2tt2+t+12=c(2t+1)

From the first equation, we obtain c=12. Substituting c=12 into the second equality, we get t2+t+12=12(2t+1)t2=0t=0.

Therefore, r and r′ are parallel at the point corresponding to t=0.

Finally, since r(0)=e0i+(02+0+12)j=i+12j, we conclude that r(t) and r′(t) are parallel at the point (1,12).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Parallel to Another Vector
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)={e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =c(2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =2c{e}^{2t}\,i+c(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j$ gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}=2c{e}^{2t} \\ {t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2}=c(2t+1)\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain $c=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting $c=\frac{1}{2}$ into the second equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(2t+1) \\ {t}^{2} & =0 \\ t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel at the point corresponding to $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & ={e}^{0}\,i+({0}^{2}+0+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =i+\frac{1}{2}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,\frac{1}{2}).$

Question 18
?

Given the curve r(t)=⟨4t−t2,t3⟩, find all points at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector ⟨2,1⟩.

a
(−5,−1) and (0,0)
b
(3,1) and (43,59)
c
(0,0) and (209,827)
d
(43,59) and (0,0)
e
(−5,−1) and (209,827)
Submit

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨4−2t,3t²⟩ is parallel to ⟨2,1⟩ when 4−2t=6t². Thus (3t−2)(t+1)=0, giving t=2/3 or t=−1. The corresponding points are (20/9,8/27) and (−5,−1), matching option e.

after.name: Question 18
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨4t-{t}^{2},{t}^{3}⟩,$ find all points at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨2,1⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨2,1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨2,1⟩ \\ ⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =c⟨2,1⟩ \\ ⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =⟨2c,c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}4-2t=2c \\ 3{t}^{2}=c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=2-t.$ Substituting in the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2} & =2-t \\ 3{t}^{2}+t-2 & =0 \\ (3t-2)(t+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨2,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the points corresponding to $t=-1,\frac{2}{3}.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨4(-1)-(-1)^{2},(-1)^{3}⟩=⟨-5,-1⟩ \\ r(\frac{2}{3}) & =⟨4(\frac{2}{3})-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2},{(\frac{2}{3})}^{3}⟩=⟨\frac{20}{9},\frac{8}{27}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨2,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(-5,-1)$ and $(\frac{20}{9},\frac{8}{27}).$

Question 18
?

Given the curve r(t)=⟨4t−t2,t3⟩, find all points at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector ⟨2,1⟩.

a
(−5,−1) and (0,0)
b
(3,1) and (43,59)
c
(0,0) and (209,827)
d
(43,59) and (0,0)
e
(−5,−1) and (209,827)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t): r′(t)=⟨ddt(4t−t2),ddt(t3)⟩=⟨4−2t,3t2⟩

The vectors r′(t) and ⟨0,1,3⟩ are parallel for some specific value t0 of the parameter t if and only if there exists a constant c such that r′(t0)=c⟨2,1⟩. So, we have

r′(t)=c⟨2,1⟩⟨4−2t,3t2⟩=c⟨2,1⟩⟨4−2t,3t2⟩=⟨2c,c⟩.

Equating the components gives: {4−2t=2c3t2=c

From the first equation, we obtain that c=2−t. Substituting in the second equation, we get 3t2=2−t3t2+t−2=0(3t−2)(t+1)=0.

Therefore, ⟨2,1⟩ and r′ are parallel only at the points corresponding to t=−1,23.

Finally, since r(−1)=⟨4(−1)−(−1)2,(−1)3⟩=⟨−5,−1⟩r(23)=⟨4(23)−(23)2,(23)3⟩=⟨209,827⟩ we conclude that ⟨2,1⟩ and r′(t) are parallel at the points (−5,−1) and (209,827).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Parallel to Another Vector
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨4t-{t}^{2},{t}^{3}⟩,$ find all points at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨2,1⟩.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨2,1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨2,1⟩ \\ ⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =c⟨2,1⟩ \\ ⟨4-2t,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =⟨2c,c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}4-2t=2c \\ 3{t}^{2}=c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=2-t.$ Substituting in the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2} & =2-t \\ 3{t}^{2}+t-2 & =0 \\ (3t-2)(t+1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨2,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the points corresponding to $t=-1,\frac{2}{3}.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨4(-1)-(-1)^{2},(-1)^{3}⟩=⟨-5,-1⟩ \\ r(\frac{2}{3}) & =⟨4(\frac{2}{3})-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2},{(\frac{2}{3})}^{3}⟩=⟨\frac{20}{9},\frac{8}{27}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨2,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(-5,-1)$ and $(\frac{20}{9},\frac{8}{27}).$

Given the curve r(t)=⟨t,t3+5,2t+2⟩, t∈(0,∞), find all of the points at which r′(t) and r(t) are parallel.

a
 (0,5,2) and (3,32,8)
b
(2,13,6)
c
 (0,5,2)
d
 (1,6,4) and (2,13,6)
e
(1,6,4)
Submit

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨1/(2√t),3t²,2⟩. If r(t)=c r'(t), the first component gives c=2t. The third then requires 2t+2=4t, so t=1. The second component also holds: 1³+5=2(1)·3(1)²=6. Thus the only point is (1,6,4), option e.

after.name: Question 19
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\sqrt{t}\,,\,{t}^{3}+5\,,\,2t+2⟩,$ $t\in (0,\infty ),$ find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+5),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+2)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},\,3{t}^{2},\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ ⟨\sqrt{t},\,{t}^{3}+5,\,2t+2⟩ & =c\,⟨\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},\,3{t}^{2},\,2⟩ \\ ⟨\sqrt{t},\,{t}^{3}+5,\,2t+2⟩ & =⟨\frac{c}{2\sqrt{t}},\,3c{t}^{2},\,2c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{t}=\frac{c}{2\sqrt{t}} \\ {t}^{3}+5=3c{t}^{2} \\ 2t+2=2c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=2t.$ Substituting into the third equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2t+2 & =2\cdot (2t) \\ 2t+2 & =4t \\ 2t-2 & =0 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This satisfies also the second equation ${t}^{3}+5=3c{t}^{2}.$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$ These values also satisfy the second equation. 

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨\sqrt{1}\,,\,{1}^{3}+5\,,\,2(1)+2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,6,\,4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,6,4).$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ ⟨\sqrt{t},\,{t}^{3}+5,\,2t+2⟩ & =c\,⟨\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},\,3{t}^{2},\,2⟩ \\ ⟨\sqrt{t},\,{t}^{3}+5,\,2t+2⟩ & =⟨\frac{c}{2\sqrt{t}},\,3c{t}^{2},\,2c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{t}=\frac{c}{2\sqrt{t}} \\ {t}^{3}+5=3c{t}^{2} \\ 2t+2=2c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=2t.$ Substituting into the third equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2t+2 & =2\cdot (2t) \\ 2t+2 & =4t \\ 2t-2 & =0 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This satisfies also the second equation ${t}^{3}+5=3c{t}^{2}.$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$ These values also satisfy the second equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨\sqrt{1}\,,\,{1}^{3}+5\,,\,2(1)+2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,6,\,4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,6,4).$

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨5t⁴,8t³⟩. Parallelism requires 8t³=(4/5)(5t⁴)=4t⁴. Since t>0, division by 4t³ gives t=2. Then r(2)=(24,26), matching option c.

after.name: Question 20
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{5}-8,2{t}^{4}-6⟩,$ $t\in (0,\infty )$, find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{5}-8),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{4}-6)⟩ \\  & =⟨5{t}^{4},8{t}^{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩ \\ ⟨5{t}^{4},8{t}^{3}⟩ & =c⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩ \\ ⟨5{t}^{4},8{t}^{3}⟩ & =⟨c,\frac{4c}{5}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}5{t}^{4}=c \\ 8{t}^{3}=\frac{4c}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=5{t}^{4}.$ Substituting $c=5{t}^{4}$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8{t}^{3} & =\frac{4(5{t}^{4})}{5} \\ 8{t}^{3}-4{t}^{4} & =0 \\ 4{t}^{3}(2-t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (0,\infty )$, the only solution is $t=2.$ 

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨(2)^{5}-8,2(2)^{4}-6⟩=⟨24,26⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(24,26).$

content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{5}-8,2{t}^{4}-6⟩,$ $t\in (0,\infty )$, find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{5}-8),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{4}-6)⟩ \\  & =⟨5{t}^{4},8{t}^{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩ \\ ⟨5{t}^{4},8{t}^{3}⟩ & =c⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩ \\ ⟨5{t}^{4},8{t}^{3}⟩ & =⟨c,\frac{4c}{5}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}5{t}^{4}=c \\ 8{t}^{3}=\frac{4c}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=5{t}^{4}.$ Substituting $c=5{t}^{4}$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8{t}^{3} & =\frac{4(5{t}^{4})}{5} \\ 8{t}^{3}-4{t}^{4} & =0 \\ 4{t}^{3}(2-t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (0,\infty )$, the only solution is $t=2.$ 

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨(2)^{5}-8,2(2)^{4}-6⟩=⟨24,26⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,\frac{4}{5}⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(24,26).$
